statement: A standard interval of length n≥0 is the poset category on {0,…,n} generated by one chosen directed transition between each consecutive pair i−1,i.
notes: The adjacent-arrow labels i,i+1 in condition(a) are corrected in brackets by the edition itself; use i−1,i.

statement: Standard intervals of length n correspond bijectively to sign words in {+,-}^n; there are exactly 2^n.
repair: Freeness of the oriented path constructs the category; unique directed routes imply thinness. Commentary: A directed interval with two orders.

statement: The source and target of a standard interval are its positional endpoints 0 and n, irrespective of categorical arrow directions.
An orientation is the positional total order; preceding/following vertices refer to this order, not to the categorical partial order.
Transition arrows are ordered by their indices 1,…,n; immediate successor/predecessor means index difference +1/−1.
For E⊆Z, integer-connected components are the equivalence classes generated by consecutive integers; i<j lie in one component iff [i,j]⊆E.
notes: The source proves the equivalent characterization by identifying a connected string of integers.

statement: A chain of transitions is an integer-connected subset of {1,…,n}; a nonempty chain of length l has consecutive indices i,…,i+l−1.
notes: The text calls the empty set connected. An empty chain has no uniquely determined domain or initial sign; later endpoint statements require a nonempty chain.

statement: A transition chain is composable iff all its arrows have the same sign; composition uses increasing index order for + and reverse order for −.
notes: The reverse composite is supplied by an edition bracket.

statement: Maximal composable chains are the connected components of the positive and negative transition subsets.
Structural chains partition the transitions into ordered constant-sign runs C1,…,Cr; r is the useful length.
notes: For n>0, 1≤r≤n; for n=0, r=0, as the text subsequently specifies.

statement: Consecutive structural chains have opposite signs; initial and final direction agree iff useful length r is odd, for nonempty intervals.
Initial/final direction is the sign of the first/last transition or structural chain; these directions are undefined for the singleton.
As printed, composable transition chains correspond to all full subcategories isomorphic to [k].
gap_or_error: A full chain subcategory may skip ambient vertices, so it need not be the domain of a contiguous chain of transitions.
repair: Restrict to full subcategories on contiguous positional intervals inside one run. The full subcategory {0,2}⊆[2] is a counterexample to the unrestricted correspondence.
references: Commentary: Intrinsic endpoints and the scope of rigidity
notes: The source immediately strengthens this to maximal chains; that additional error is audited separately.

statement: The ordinal category [k] has only the identity automorphism.
repair: An order automorphism preserves the least element and each successive element.

statement: As printed, maximal composable transition chains of length k correspond exactly to vertex-injective functors [k]→I.
gap_or_error: Injective functors can have nonmaximal and noncontiguous images.
repair: An injective functor picks k+1 vertices in a single structural interval, in categorical order. A maximal chain corresponds to its entire structural interval. Example [1]→[2], 0↦0,1↦2.
references: Commentary: Intrinsic endpoints and the scope of rigidity
notes: Confirmed visually in edition p3/PDF5; this is an edition/source overstatement, not a transcription fault.

statement: A vertex-injective functor [k]→I is fully faithful and a monomorphism of categories.
repair: Its image is a categorical chain. Thinness makes faithfulness automatic; order on [k] and the absence of reverse arrows give fullness. Injectivity on objects and arrows gives monicity.

statement: For k≥1 a vertex-injective [k]→I is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing in the positional order, according to the direction of its containing structural interval.
repair: All image vertices lie in a unique constant-sign run; functoriality orders them in its categorical direction.

statement: The ordinal [k] is an interval of length k and useful length 1 if k>0, and useful length0 if k=0.
An interval category is any category isomorphic to a standard interval.
Proposition1(a): in an interval of positive length, s is an endpoint iff one of I/s,s\I is punctual and the other is an ordinal category [j].
repair: At an endpoint there is one arm; at a noncritical interior vertex both strict slices are nonempty; at a critical interior vertex the nonpunctual slice has two incomparable arms.
references: Commentary: Intrinsic endpoints and the scope of rigidity

statement: The proposed intrinsic criterion distinguishing the source endpoint is left incomplete in the edition.
gap_or_error: The sentence ends after s\I and has no completed mathematical assertion.
repair: Choosing an orientation, equivalently one endpoint as source, is necessary; no purely categorical source distinction exists for a symmetric interval.
notes: Do not assign a truth value to the unfinished sentence or silently complete it.

statement: Proposition1(b), as printed: every endofunctor I→I fixing both endpoints is the identity.
gap_or_error: An endofunctor may collapse an intermediate vertex while preserving the endpoints.
repair: Replace endofunctor by automorphism, which is all the subsequent reconstruction and corollary require. Counterexample [2] with values(0,0,2). A stronger exact repair is that the endofunctor statement holds iff I is reduced.
references: Commentary: Intrinsic endpoints and the scope of rigidity; The exact endpoint rigidity criterion
notes: No earlier published erratum located in the sources checked; proof and counterexample are supplied here.

statement: The automorphism group of an interval has at most two elements; a nonidentity automorphism interchanges its endpoints.
gap_or_error: The stated Proposition1(b) is too strong, but the proof is valid for automorphisms.
repair: Use preservation of indecomposable arrows: the underlying path has at most the identity and reflection.
references: Commentary: Intrinsic endpoints and the scope of rigidity

statement: An interval is symmetric if it has a nonidentity automorphism, necessarily interchanging the two endpoints.
Commentary: an interval admits only the identity endpoint-fixing endofunctor iff it is reduced.
repair: For reduced intervals every vertex increment has absolute value≤1 and endpoints force all increments+1. If a run has length≥2, collapse a noncritical vertex onto its positional predecessor and fix all other vertices.

statement: At an interior source with adjacent constant-sign arm lengths r,s, its coslice is [r] amalgamated with [s] at their initial vertices; it is not an ordinal category. The sink case is dual.

statement: Choosing one endpoint intrinsically determines the positional order by successively recovering its neighbour in the remaining full interval.
gap_or_error: The displayed slices in the induction incorrectly retain I and i rather than the remaining interval I′ and current vertex s_i.

statement: Proposition2: for a standard interval I there is a unique standard interval J and isomorphism I→J sending target to source and source to target.
repair: J has word Rτ=(-τ_n,…,-τ_1); the isomorphism is i↦n−i. For n=0 it is the identity.

statement: The oppositely oriented interval has the same underlying category and the reverse positional orientation; this differs from the opposite category.
A nontrivial abstract interval has exactly two standard presentations by categorical isomorphisms; they induce opposite total orders and opposite orientations.
repair: Each endpoint choice gives one traversal and one standard labelling. The singleton gives one presentation.
notes: After an orientation is fixed, exactly one presentation respects it.

statement: Choosing an orientation of an interval is equivalent to choosing its source endpoint.
notes: For the singleton there is one possible choice; the two endpoints coincide.

statement: The two standard models obtained from opposite orientations agree iff the underlying interval is symmetric.
notes: Read for positive length; the singleton models agree but the automorphism group is trivial, so the strict definition of symmetric requires the nontrivial exception.

statement: The opposite category of a standard interval is the interval obtained by changing every transition sign.
The two three-vertex forks Φ1 and Ψ1 are symmetric and opposite, but not isomorphic.
repair: Each has endpoint reflection; one has a unique source and two sinks, the other a unique sink and two sources.

statement: For k>0, [k] is not symmetric but is isomorphic to its opposite category.
notes: The statement remains true for k=0 under symmetry defined by a nonidentity automorphism; [0] has trivial self-duality and one orientation.

statement: Any isomorphism from a nontrivial interval I to I^op is unique and reverses positional orientation.
repair: An isomorphism of underlying indecomposable-arrow paths is identity or reflection; identity cannot reverse a nonempty edge orientation.

statement: A nontrivial interval cannot be both symmetric and isomorphic to its opposite category.
repair: Symmetry requires τ_i=-τ_{n+1-i}, whereas self-duality requires τ_i=τ_{n+1-i}.
references: Commentary: Reversal and categorical duality
notes: The edition supplies a singleton exception in brackets. Under the earlier strict definition of symmetric by a nonidentity automorphism, the singleton is not symmetric; both sign-word tests are merely vacuous there.

statement: For k>0 the notation [k]^+ and [k]^- denotes its two traversal orientations.
The domain of a nonempty transition chain with indices i,…,i+l−1 is the full vertex interval[i−1,i+l−1].
notes: An empty chain does not determine an origin; the displayed formula presupposes l>0.

statement: Structural or critical intervals are the domains of structural chains; critical vertices are their endpoints.
notes: For the singleton the later reduction convention treats its unique vertex as critical; the empty family of structural runs alone would not define it.

statement: For structural lengths l1,…,lr, the structural vertex intervals are [0,l1],[l1,l1+l2],…; successive ones meet in one endpoint and are positionally ordered.
notes: The source I instead of I_i in the order comparison is an edition slip.

statement: Proposition3 as printed: s is critical iff I\{s} is the coproduct of (I/s)\{s} and (s\I)\{s}.
gap_or_error: Vertices incomparable with s are absent from both slices.
repair: Local repair: replace I\{s} by the full subcategory of vertices comparable with s, minus s. Global repair: an internal s is critical iff deleting s separates the two positional sides. Counterexample to printed statement: I=(0→1←2→3), s=0.
references: Commentary: Critical vertices and the missing complement
notes: Both valid replacements are proved completely here; the edition already corrects the duplicated I/s notation for I″.

statement: Footnote3: s is critical iff no arrow joins a strict categorical predecessor of s to a strict categorical successor.
repair: If both classes are nonempty, composition p→s→q supplies such an arrow. One class is empty precisely at a source or sink, i.e. a critical vertex.
references: Commentary: Critical vertices and the missing complement
notes: This is a local criterion, weaker than the printed global decomposition. Endpoints are included; singleton by convention.

statement: Proposition4: for i<j, existence of an arrow in either direction, membership in one structural interval, and the full category on[i,j] being an ordinal[j−i] are equivalent.
repair: An arrow exists exactly when all intervening signs agree; that is precisely a single constant-sign run.
references: Commentary: A directed interval with two orders

statement: Two objects of any category are directly connected if there is a morphism in at least one direction between them.
Proposition5(a): every connected component of a full subcategory of an interval is an interval; the induced positional order is an orientation.
repair: Sort selected vertices. A missing critical vertex separates; otherwise consecutive selected vertices are joined inside one structural run and generate the full subcategory.

statement: Proposition5(b): for a subset J with at least two vertices and extremes i<j, its full subcategory is an interval iff it contains every critical vertex of I in[i,j].
gap_or_error: The source invokes the false global form of Proposition3 for the necessity argument.
repair: Use the valid positional-cut criterion. Sufficiency follows by composing transitions between consecutive selected vertices.
references: Commentary: Full subintervals and canonical reduction

statement: A subinterval is a nonempty full connected subcategory of an interval.
notes: The source identifies full connected subcategories with intervals. Empty categories are excluded from interval categories.

statement: Footnote4: every subcategory of an interval which is itself an interval is full.

repair: Counterexample in[2]: keep all objects and only0→2,1→2. This is the interval0→2←1 but omits0→1. Later fullness claims need additional increasingness or equivalent conditions.

repair: Necessity and sufficiency follow directly from Proposition5(b), proving minimality.
references: Commentary: Full subintervals and canonical reduction

statement: An interval is reduced or irredundant if all its vertices are critical, equivalently every structural run has length1.

statement: A positive-length oriented reduced interval is determined up to oriented isomorphism by its length and initial sign.
repair: Its signs alternate; for length0 there is only the empty word and no initial sign.

Proposition6: a subinterval with extremes i<j is reduced iff every one of its internal selected vertices is critical in the ambient interval.
repair: At ambient noncritical vertices the nearest selected adjacent arrows compose; at ambient critical vertices they form a turn.

statement: The full category on all critical vertices is a reduced subinterval, denoted I_red, and has length equal to the useful length of I.
repair: Retain endpoints of all constant-sign runs; each run becomes one transition.
references: Commentary: Full subintervals and canonical reduction
notes: The length equality is immediate from the definitions; singleton uses the convention above.

statement: For an oriented interval I and category X, a path of type I is a functor I→X and the path category is Fun(I,X), with natural transformations as arrows.
An oriented interval has a canonical oriented isomorphism to its standard model, allowing identification of the corresponding fixed-type path categories.
repair: Use the unique increasing enumeration of the finite vertex set.

notes: Edition p9/PDF11, retained as an edition slip.

statement: A functor I_tau→X is equivalent to a choice of n+1 objects a0,…,an and n arrows between consecutive objects in directions prescribed by tau.
repair: I_tau is the free category on its transition graph, so the assignment extends uniquely.

statement: A morphism in an interval between nonconsecutive vertices lies in one structural run and maps to the corresponding composite under every path functor.

For the direct one-edge shape, Ch_[1]^+(X) is the arrow category of X.
The two orientations of the one-edge interval yield canonically isomorphic path categories, with source and target exchanged.
The two orientations of[2] give composable pairs in opposite traversal orders, again with endpoint-swapping isomorphism of path categories.

repair: For X=(a<t>b), the span category has9 objects and the cospan category11.

Commentary: for a finite poset X the numbers of span and cospan diagrams are respectively sum_x|up(x)|² and sum_x|down(x)|²; for the three-vertex cospan these are9 and11.
repair: Choose the middle vertex and its two comparable endpoints independently.

notes: A fully calculated elementary example of the known zigzag interval-decomposition theorem.

statement: A path is formally the data of an oriented indexing interval and a functor, i.e.(omega,c); fixing the orientation is part of fixing its type.
The fixed-type path category has endpoint functor(sigma,beta):Fun(I,X)→X×X, given by restriction along epsilon→I from the discrete two-object category.

Passing to standard words eliminates automorphisms of the oriented indexing shape.
